newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai reforms hailed abroad, criticised at home.
newsitem.headline: Thai reforms hailed abroad, criticised at home.

text.p: Thailand's decision to adopt tough measures to revive its economy and debt-ridden financial sector won foreign support but provoked heated criticism at home on Wednesday.

The International Monetary Fund, Japan, and the United States welcomed the sweeping $12-$15 billion economic package that included a value added tax (VAT) hike, government budget cuts and suspension of nearly two-thirds of the country's 91 finance companies.

"I found particularly appropriate the adoption of a comprehensive restructuring of troubled financial institutions, as this is essential to lay the basis for the re-establishment of a sound financial sector," said IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus.
Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said the suspension of finance firms and the VAT tax hike would stabilise markets and contribute to longer-term development of the Thai economy.

Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh, however, faced strong domestic opposition to his plans to close finance houses which had borrowed heavily from the government this year to ease cashflow problems.

"The government made a mistake in suspending another 42 firms. It used its last card for shoring up what already was low confidence in the government," said Kitti Limsakul, economics lecturer at Chulalongkorn University.

Central bank governor Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi said on Tuesday suspended finance companies, hurt by over-exposure to a collapsed property sector, had tapped a combined 430 billion baht ($13.9 billion) of bailout loans from the authorities.
Most analysts were surprised by the big bailout loans. Don Hanna of Goldman Sachs told Reuters Financial Television the loans amounted to about 10 percent of gross domestic product.
"They have not clarified how they're going to allocate the losses of finance companies and that would be critical for restoring domestic and external financial confidence," he said.

Analysts said the market also awaited details of Chavalit's budget cut. The premier said on Tuesday he would trim up to 100 billion baht off 1997/98 (October-September) state spending if necessary to help the government balance its budget.

Thailand's severe economic slowdown would leave the government with its first budget deficits in a decade in the current and next fiscal years. The Thai economy is projected to grow at its slowest in over a decade this year.

Nicholas Bibby, economist at Chase Manhattan Bank in Hong Kong, told Reuters Financial Television: "We still need to look at the actual budget cut. What are going to be cut...IMF is pretty much insistent on a budget cut of at least 110 billion baht from next year's budget."
Analysts said although the IMF-backed bailout plan may boost the baht's stability, the government had lost credibility for its vague budget plan and temporary closure of finance firms.

"The package is an overkill. The government should not have moved simultaneously on the baht and financial institution issues. It should first set an austerity precedent by cutting its budget," Kitti of Chulalongkorn University said.
After the government floated the baht last month the currency lost more than 20 percent of its value.
Kitti said the fallout of the reform package would shake the Chavalit government. It could have taken a more discreet Asian approach in dealing with finance sector problems," he said.

The Bangkok Post said in a front-page editorial: "Let's not forget how this country wound up in this sorry debacle in the first place. Politicians of all shades, including General Chavalit, are to blame. They have allowed this country to surrender its economic sovereignty because of their gross mismanagement over the past several years."
